title: MOS Loads and Cascode Pairs
intro: Resistors take area and give gains that are hard to set, so integrated differential pairs usually use transistor loads. The half circuit gives the gain of each version directly.

blocks.text: Each load is a diode-connected PMOS, which looks like $1/g_{mP}$ to AC ground:

blocks.alt: Differential pair M1, M2 with tail ISS. Each drain connects to a diode-connected PMOS load, M3 and M4, whose gates are tied to their own drains and whose sources go to VDD. Outputs X and Y are at the drains.
blocks.caption: Diode-connected loads: a well-defined but low gain, and the output CM level is fixed at $V_{DD} - |V_{GSP}|$.

blocks.text: The gain is a ratio of device sizes, so it is stable, but it is small. For a fixed current and input device, raising the gain means shrinking $(W/L)_P$, which raises $|V_{GSP} - V_{THP}|$ and lowers the output CM level. Gain, output swing and input CM range therefore trade against each other. The upside is that the loads define the output CM level, $V_{DD} - |V_{GSP}|$, with no extra circuitry.
With PMOS current sources as loads the gain is that of a CS stage with an active load:

In nanometer processes this is only about 5 to 10. The output CM level is no longer defined by anything: it is set by the small difference between the NMOS and PMOS currents across two high resistances, so a high-gain fully differential stage needs common-mode feedback (see the op-amp pages).

One way to bias the PMOS loads without a separate $V_b$ is to join the two outputs through two equal large resistors $R_1$ and drive both PMOS gates from their midpoint N. At DC each PMOS is then effectively diode-connected through $R_1$, so $V_X = V_Y = V_N = V_{DD} - |V_{GS3,4}|$. For a differential output N does not move, so the half circuit has $R_1$ to AC ground:

blocks.caption: Negligible gain loss if $R_1 \gg r_{o1} \parallel r_{o3}$.

blocks.text: Raising the gain with auxiliary current sources

The gain of the diode-loaded pair is limited by $g_{mP}$. Supplying most of each input transistor's current from a PMOS current source in parallel with the diode lets the diode carry less current; at the same overdrive its W/L, and therefore $g_{mP}$, falls in proportion. If the extra sources carry 80 percent of $I_{SS}/2$, the diode current and $g_{mP}$ drop fivefold and the gain rises fivefold (ignoring $r_o$).

The diode loads still cost at least $V_{TH}$ of headroom, so a better version uses resistors as the loads with PMOS sources alongside. Each output can now rise to $V_{DD} - |V_{GS} - V_{TH}|_{P}$ instead of $V_{DD} - |V_{TH}|$, and since $R_D$ carries only 20 percent of the current it can be five times larger for the same output CM level:

blocks.alt: Differential pair whose drains X and Y each connect to a resistor RD to VDD and, in parallel, to a PMOS current source M5 or M6 with gates tied to Vb. Each PMOS is marked as carrying 0.4 ISS.
blocks.caption: Resistor loads with auxiliary PMOS current sources. With long PMOS devices $r_{oP} \gg r_{oN}$ and the gain approaches $g_{mN}(R_D \parallel r_{oN})$; as $R_D \to \infty$ the circuit becomes the current-source-loaded pair.

blocks.text: To go beyond $g_m r_o$, cascode both the input devices and the loads, which gives a differential version of the cascode stage. With input M1, NMOS cascode M3, PMOS cascode M5 and PMOS source M7 in each half, the half circuit gives
The gain rises by roughly a factor $g_m r_o$, paid for with two more stacked devices of headroom. This telescopic structure, and the CM feedback it needs, return in the op-amp chapter.
Stacking two cross-connected pairs on a third pair gives a variable-gain amplifier and analog multiplier; it has its own page, The Gilbert Cell.

blocks.title: Diode-connected load gain
blocks.text: A pair has $(W/L)_1 = 40$ and diode-connected PMOS loads with $(W/L)_3 = 10$ at equal current; $\mu_n$ is 3 times $\mu_p$. Find the gain.

blocks.title: Cascoding a current-source-loaded pair
blocks.text: Every NMOS has $g_m = 1\text{ mS}$, $r_o = 20\text{ k}\Omega$; every PMOS has $g_m = 1\text{ mS}$, $r_o = 25\text{ k}\Omega$. Compare the gain of the simple current-source-loaded pair with the fully cascoded pair.
solution: Cascoded: NMOS side $g_m r_o^2 = 1\text{ mS} \cdot 20\text{ k} \cdot 20\text{ k} = 400\text{ k}\Omega$; PMOS side $1\text{ mS} \cdot 25\text{ k} \cdot 25\text{ k} = 625\text{ k}\Omega$; in parallel 244 kΩ, so $|A_v| = 244$.

blocks.title: Self-biased loads
blocks.text: In the self-biased current-source-loaded pair, $g_{m1} = 1\text{ mS}$, $r_{o1} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, $r_{o3} = 25\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_1 = 100\text{ k}\Omega$. What gain is lost to $R_1$?
solution: With it: $11.1\text{ k} \parallel 100\text{ k} = 10.0\text{ k}\Omega$, so $|A_v| = 10.0$, about 10 percent less.

blocks.title: How much auxiliary current?
blocks.text: A diode-loaded pair has a gain of 3. The designer adds PMOS current sources that carry 75 percent of each input device's current and resizes the diodes to keep the same overdrive. Ignoring $r_o$, what is the new gain?
solution: The diodes now carry a quarter of the current. At constant overdrive $g_m = 2I_D/|V_{GS} - V_{TH}|$, so $g_{mP}$ falls fourfold.
